To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) The incidence of venous thromboembolisms in children with cancer varies between studies, (ii) The incidence of thromboses in children is higher than previously appreciated, (iii) The risk of thrombosis in children is higher in those with malignancies and (iv) The risk of venous thrombosis in childhood is higher than in adults.
the incidence of thrombophilia and thrombosis is high in children with cancer and that the treatment of such disease in children is complex.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the understanding of the pathophysiology of thrombotic disease in the child with cancer, the role of the new generation of anticoagulant therapies in the treatment of this condition and finally the development of novel therapeutic strategies to prevent thrombotic disease.
understanding the pathophysiology of thrombosis in children with cancer, and the use of novel anticoagulants in this patient group.
the understanding the mechanisms of thrombotic disease in children with cancer and the development of appropriate therapeutic interventions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

children with cancer have a higher risk of developing thrombotic complications than the general paediatric and adult population and this is related to the type of malignancy, the site of disease and the treatment modality.
children with cancer are more at risk of developing TE than their non-cancer counterparts.

TE is a common and serious complication of cancer in the paediatric population and the incidence is likely to increase with the increasing survival rates of these children.

we have a better understanding of how the anticoagulant pathways work and we now have the tools to manipulate them to treat thrombosis in children.
the risk of thrombosis in children with cancer can be reduced by using a combination of risk stratification, prophylaxis and treatment of the disease.
we have made significant advances in our knowledge of thrombotic complications in childhood cancer and the treatment of this condition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children with cancer are not a homogeneous group and that there is no single thrombosis risk factor or thrombotic phenotype that applies to the entire group of cancer patients.
the risk of TE in children is higher than previously thought and that we should be more aware of this in our clinical practice.

there is a high risk of TE in children and young people with cancer and the majority is due to indwelling catheters, but there is an increasing number who are developing TE in the absence of any identifiable risk factors.
